utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Nikolic, good morning to you. I welcome you back on behalf of the Trial Chamber. I hope you are feeling somewhat better. I gave instructions that you change places with Mr. Popovic. You sit outside. The registrar, through -- on the advice of the Detention Unit doctor advised -- please remain seated -- advised us that you may need, from time to time, to walk around a little bit. Any time you need that, please draw our attention, and we will of course allow you to do that. Not in the courtroom, obviously, but anything you need -- and if you are not feeling well and would like to retire and go back to the Detention Unit, please let us know. So all the accused are here today. Yeah, the -- in the -- in one monitor we are receiving the transcript; in the other monitor, at least I am not -- no, and my colleagues aren't receiving anything. So -- and -- you have the same problem. Yeah. Anyway, for the time being, we can -- we can continue. For the record, Ms. Condon is not here, as per the statement by Mr. Zivanovic yesterday. Mr. Haynes is not here. Mr. Sarapa, is there a problem with Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Josse is also not here. Mr. Krgovic, I think you gave an explanation yesterday. That is still valid. Otherwise we are a full house. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Before we bring in -- or shall we first finish with Ms. Frease and then deal with some of the motions that have arrived since yesterday, something like 150 pages worth of reading. Let's start with Ms. Frease and then continue afterwards. In the meantime, if you can -- because unfortunately we don't have transcript scrolling in e-court, yeah. Yeah, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could be excused for a moment, I see that Mr. Nikolic is here. If I may go work on some witness issues to see if there is anything we can do to fill some space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. McCloskey. And I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will continue your testimony in chief in part again today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No cross-examination. May I just recall that you have already made an undertaking with this Trial Chamber that you will be testifying the truth; you have made a solemn declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which you don't need to repeat, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, president, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll be able to pick up where we left off nearly a week ago. Do you recall testifying about a project which involved your review, organisation and analysis of certain intercepted communications that were received by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in conducting these various functions, did you have occasion to come into possession and review original notebooks containing these intercepted transcriptions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Vanderpuye, because I want it make sure that there is no objection on the part of Defence counsel that we proceed even though -- even though the -- the e-court transcript is not yet on. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We don't object to proceeding, but I do object to the leading question that was put to the witness. This witness, I understand, Ms. Frease, is obviously intelligent and sophisticated. He can just ask her what she's reviewed, if anything, and not put that it was original notebooks or not. That's what we're hoping to learn from her. So I'm not going to object the entire time during the direct examination, but I think at the very least with this witness, there should be absolutely no leading by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't consider it a leading question. I mean asking her whether she came into possession and review original notebooks containing these intercepted transcriptions, I mean is not a leading question. In any case, that question was put to her last time. I remember it quite vividly and she answered it. She even stated in chief that she had an occasion to review these notebooks when she came together with someone else in possession of them while they were still in Yugoslavia. I mean in -- over there anyway. So I don't think there is a need to repeat that question in any case. I suggest you pass straight to the substance of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do recall -- and you will correct me if I'm wrong, that you testified previously about coming into possession of a number of materials?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like -- I would like to initially focus your attention on the printed material that you came into possession of. And can you tell us whether or not you came into possession of printed material relating to these intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when I say printed, I mean separate and apart from handwritten transcriptions?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And, first, can you tell us what these printed versions of intercepts actually are?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In April of 1998, we -- the Office of the Prosecutor came into possession of printed -- well, printouts that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the 2nd Corps had provided to -- to the office. And these were -- it was about 550 pages of printed conversations that looked like they originated from a couple of different sources; from the military and then also from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not these particular printouts contained complete versions of the intercepts they purportedly contained?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't -- it's a little -- it's a little tricky to answer, so let me explain. They were complete in the sense that the substance was the -- was the same. But because they were printouts they -- and they were an analytical tool that was used by the army, they -- in the process, what we learned was that the army had taken off sometimes the -- well, always had taken off the headers that -- of the reports that they had sent to their headquarters. So this was very much a working document for them about events on the ground so that they could more easily analyse the material contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not -- well, first of all, how is it that you came to the conclusion that the headers, for example, were taken off?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later when we saw the electronic printouts of the complete reports that the army and the police sent to their headquarters, that was when it became clear that -- that a lot of that sort of identifying material had been taken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you refer to identifying material, are you referring to things such as the location or direction or things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is a direct question. You can ask her what she's referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. When you refer to identifying material, what material are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the header, sometimes the direction, sometimes the azimuth or other -- other bits of information that the operators would have recorded when they sent their messages to their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness ERN 0072-7550, please. I just wondered if I could have that placed on the ELMO so everybody could see what we're talking about. Thank you. Ms. Frease, do you recognise this object?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the -- the original binder of printed material that -- that the Office of the Prosecutor received in April of 1998, and it was the -- it was the material that we really started to use to analyse the intercepted communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you open the binder, please. Okay. I just wonder if you could flip over a couple of pages so the Court and Defence counsel can see what you are talking about when you refer to these old printouts. The one displayed now on the ELMO is 0072-7552, and could you tell us in substance -- well, generally when you referred to the header being missing or information not being present on this, could you describe what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Normally when the -- we learned later that when the army -- when the units from the two different sites sent the intercepted communication to their 2 Corps headquarters, they always put a header on the top of the -- of the report containing the various conversations. And the header just was directed to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the 2 Corps, and then essentially the communication started. Now, there is -- on this particular document, there is a date of the 9th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was it always the case that the date would appear in these particular types of printouts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just go down to the bottom of the page on the ELMO so the Court can see that? Now, at the bottom of the page, there appears to be a line on this particular page which goes right to the base and it appears that there is a photocopy mark right below it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, is this -- could you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photocopy. These are all photocopies of material that came off of like a dot-matrix printer where the sheets, they are old -- you know the old kind of printouts where the pages -- the document would print out to the bottom of the page and then there would be a perforated edge where it would tear at and then the communication would continue. But in the process of tearing those pages, oftentimes then in photocopying them, a few lines could be missing from the bottom of the page or even the top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that an unusual occurrence with respect to these types of printouts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was very common.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I see on the page that you've just turned over to, there are -- there is a capitalised printing in this particular section of the report.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Versus the top of the page where there is, I guess, sentence case printing with respect to that. Could you tell the Court what the distinction is between these two types of casing in the context of these reports?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reports that were printed in all capital letters came from the police, and that was one way that we were able to quickly distinguish who the source was on a particular document, at least at this early stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say the police, the police in general or any particular section of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit that was also based at the northern site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the presence of these reports within the context of these printouts an unusual occurrence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in fact, is there -- is there another way to distinguish between communications that originated, as you say, with the police at the northern site versus those that originated with the 2nd Corps unit?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police always put this sort of a header on it, that started off with, "On the above-mentioned day, from the direction of" and then they would mention the direction and then they would identify the frequency. I can just point to it here. And then the channel. And then they would say at this hour they recorded a conversation between -- if they could -- if they understood and they could hear who the conversants were, the participants were, then they would indicate those names. If they didn't know who the participants were, then they would indicate X and Y or something like that. But the police unit up there always started their conversations with this kind of a header, which was different from the military -- from the military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us if you have any particular knowledge how it is that these reports came to be apparently in the possession of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They shared information. The units up at the northern site shared information. Well, I guess also the southern site. The information was filtered and then -- and then the army and the police shared -- shared all of their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, do you know approximately when this material was transferred into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was late April 1998. April 24th, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know who was involved in the receipt of this item?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A former member of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you want me to mention him by name?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, I think --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Peter Nicholson.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know where this occurred, where this transfer actually took place?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If I may, I'd like to draw your attention to other documents, if we could. Now, you mentioned previously these intercepts from the police located at the northern site -- state -- is that state security?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know whether or not the Office of the Prosecutor actually received any printouts from the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell us the circumstances, if you know, under which that material came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A -- many -- many conversations were handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know the circumstances under which this particular transfer occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were handed over to Jean-Rene Ruez in July of that year, late July of that year, I think the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review any documents in confirming the circumstances of this transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have please PO2400 on the ELMO. I'm sorry, in e-court. All right. I think we have it. Ms. Frease, can you see this?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a receipt from the agency for investigation and documentation which is the police, the secret police. The name of the -- it was renamed after the war ended. It's their document number 1406 dated the 27th of July, 1999. And says that it was handed over to members of the -- of the -- of an investigative team from the International Criminal Court on that date, and then it provides a detailed list of all of the reports that were handed over that day. One thing that I forgot to add, in looking at the -- that printed document that we -- that we just looked at, for the police reports, one of the other identifying factors for the police reports was that they always numbered the -- their conversations. So these numbers, like that start with 365 from the 21st of June, 1995, that report number would have appeared on that particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say would have appeared on that, is it in the context of a header or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It was -- it was associated with a specific conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just go to -- I think the second page of this document in e-court. Okay. And can you tell us what we have -- well, first, obviously you see signatures on there, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is above the signatures following the long list of reports?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. It -- there's the next line down that starts with "Takodje". Also that they provided some radio recordings of conversations that relate to those report numbers and those report numbers are found -- relate to reports that were provided on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And does that also relate to the line following?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That line says that those are recordings on cassette that relate to the following report, the report numbers that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the ultimate line?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the last line is a 20-page diary that was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in referring to this document you are able to confirm that those items were received by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. May I focus your attention, please, on a different set of documents that you previously mentioned you had reviewed, and those relate to electronic versions of intercepted material. First, could you tell the Court what is meant by -- what an electronic version of printed material actually is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the reports that the military and the police typed up at their locations and sent to their headquarters in electronic format.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the military, can you tell us, if you know, if the Office of the Prosecutor came into possession of this electronic material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you know the circumstances under which that material came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, could you share that with us as well?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received first two diskettes from the military in -- the date is escaping me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. May I have, if I could, 65 ter 1071 displayed on the -- in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise the document that's displayed at this time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a receipt that was produced by 2 Corps headquarters in Tuzla with their reference number, and dated the 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you -- I'm sorry. Could you tell us what -- is it possible to have the translation also displayed, I guess side by side for the benefit of the Court and counsel? All right. Thank you very much. This document records the transfer of a certain two disks; it says 1.4 megabyte diskettes. Is that accurate? Is that what you received?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us by refering to the document when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the document also indicates that other material was transferred as well. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first item on the list relates to 55 notebooks in A5 format that were transferred to us containing transcripts of conversations. The second item refers to an A4-format notebook containing also transcripted conversations. The third item relates to the two diskettes and then the fourth is a shift diary, also a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These are the notebooks that you referred to earlier as original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have also PO2311 displayed in e-court for the witness, please. While we're waiting for that to load, could you tell us, if you recall, the circumstances under which you received this material, the 55 A5 notebooks and the two diskettes? Can you tell us where that occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And besides -- may we go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session all ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did there come a time that the Office of the Prosecutor received additional or other electronic files containing intercepted material relative to the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was after I had left the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if you know, can you tell us the circumstances under which that material came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in -- from documents that I reviewed, it was in December of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 1072, please, displayed in e-court? While that document is loading, could you tell us, if you know, where this occurred and who was involved from the end of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jean-Rene Ruez picked up some material, including seven diskettes of electronic versions of -- of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Do you have 65 ter 1072 now? You can see that document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this the document you referred to as having -- having relied upon in confirming the date of transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me for one moment. Just bear with me. Okay. If I could, I'd like to have the annex for -- annex number -- number 3, please, displayed for the witness. I'm going to see if I can see the ERN number. It's page 5 in English, yes. And it is page -- page -- I don't have a page number but I have an ERN number of 01085071. It appears to be page 4 in the B/C/S. Great. Thank you very much. Do you see that, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does this relate to the seven diskettes to which you referred previously?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And there is a range assigned to each diskette; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a date range.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you had an opportunity to verify that those disks, in fact, contain the information that is indicated on this report?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not had an opportunity to go through disk by disk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if we have -- well, if the Office of the Prosecutor has reports for -- within the range that is depicted on this?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And those are electronic reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had a opportunity to work with those reports in evaluating the reliability of the intercepts that you have looked at?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Have you had an opportunity to compare the information that's contained in these electronic versions of reports with the printed reports that was received by the Office of the Prosecutor sometime earlier, the ones contained in the binder that you had testified about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in comparing the two, have you found any textual discrepancies between them, aside from what you mentioned concerning the heading, direction, azimuth, things of that nature? I'm speaking specifically about the actual text of the intercepted material.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any differences between the two, other than text missing that was at the bottom or at the top of the printouts that we talked about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to determine whether the information that's contained in these electronic versions of the printout materially conformed to the original notebook transcriptions of those -- of intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did it substantially conform to the original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to direct your attention to electronic data of a different sort. Do you know if the Office of the Prosecutor came into possession of electronic data from what you've described as the police or the state security?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could tell us what the circumstances surrounding that transfer were?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That transfer also took place after I left the Office of the Prosecutor. I left in July of 2000. I believe that material was handed over in 2001, and was collected by an investigator working on this case, an investigator by the name of Jean Gagnon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have PO2399 please displayed in e-court? Okay. Thank you. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this a document that you reviewed in determining the circumstances surrounding the transfer of electronic data from the state security?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the date that's indicated here appears to be 8th of -- 28th of August, 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just scroll down for a moment, please. Okay, you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Jean Gagnon's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know -- first of all, how many disks or what kind of data this information was transferred on?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five disks are indicated in the receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And were you able to determine if this electronic data conformed to the earlier acquired hard copies that you had mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did it, in fact, conform to that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't compared the exact reports that came on those five disks to the receipt that we previously discussed. But there are certainly -- but I have seen electronic versions of the reports that are mentioned in that previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words you can match the report numbers?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Could I turn your attention to yet some other documents.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can get through this one relatively briefly. And this relates to the acquisition of the original notebooks. And can you tell us basically the circumstances under which the collection of notebooks was acquired by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a mission, a trip to the Tuzla area in March of 1998, during which time those original notebooks were found. At the time, however, the Office of the Prosecutor didn't have permission from the Bosnian authorities to take possession of those. So the notebooks were secured in the 2 Corps headquarters, and then were handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor in April, the next month, April of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I just have 65 ter 1068 displayed in e-court, please. While we're waiting for that to load, can you tell us, did the Office of the Prosecutor acquire the notebooks all at once or was that staggered over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was staggered over a period of time during the first -- we received the first batch, if you like, in April of 1998, and then two subsequent groups that we've already talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what we have displayed on e-court appears to bear your signature in the B/C/S version. Can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a receipt from the 2 Corps headquarters of the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 24th of April, 1998. And it states that -- I can't read the whole document on the screen, but that I took possession of documentation, right, that's -- there was a -- there was an annex to this document that listed the 135 documents that I took possession of on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You did, in fact, take possession of these items on that day, is that --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So this document is accurate in that regard?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 1075, please, displayed on e-court. Okay. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that -- it's -- it's an index of the notebooks that was compiled in March, during the March mission, when the notebooks were first found and identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have an independent recollection as to how many notebooks actually contain intercepted material was received among the 135 documents that were turned over?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 134 notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I would just like to turn to the last page of this document. Just for the benefit of the Court, so they can see how many documents were actually turned over and also that it does bear a signature at the bottom, so I would ask that it not be broadcast. It is not being broadcast. Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Frease. You indicated that there were 134 notebooks relating to intercepted material. And there was one additional book, I guess?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. A list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is that indicated on this particular document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's item 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it refers to a list preceded by the number 83?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what that relates to in particular, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that it's daily reports of radio -- I can't read the word on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need to zoom in so that maybe she can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to make that out?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would note on the bottom right there are -- if we can into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We've gone over already your acquisition of certain 55 A4 notebooks, one A5 notebook and a diary that was referred to in 65 ter 1071. Can you tell us, in relation to the April 1998 transfer, whether that transfer, in May of 1999, was the second transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember the circumstances under which that occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during another mission to Tuzla, and -- and we were given those documents by 2 Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did there come a time where there were other notebooks that were subsequently acquired by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, if you know, what the circumstances regarding that transfer was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also after I left, but it was, I believe, Jean-Rene Ruez picked them up in December of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that at the same time that the seven disks were transferred to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know how many notebooks were involved in relation to that transaction?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were 42, but it's indicated on the -- on the receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the condition of these notebooks following their acquisition of the -- by the Office of the Prosecutor, could you tell us whether or not any marks were placed on them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you briefly just tell us what that -- were and the circumstances surrounding them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the first 134 notebooks, they were numbered by -- during the time that Captain -- that the captain that we previously mentioned and Peter Nicholson made the inventory log. And then when I picked up the additional notebooks, the additional 50 -- 55 plus two, I also numbered those notebooks sequentially, so I started off from 135 and went up to 191 on those. There was one time in the evidence, in the ICTY evidence unit, that an evidence custodian was numbering pages inside of one notebook. We noticed that he was doing it and asked him not to do that and he wrote a note indicating that he had placed some markings inside of one notebook. Those are all the markings that I am aware of that were placed on the notebooks by people within the office of the -- or at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In addition to that, you are aware that the notebooks are Bates stamped?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And other than the markings, the placing of the numbers on the notebooks, the incident that you just recounted and the Bates stamps that were placed in the notebooks, is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Other than those things, do you know whether or not the notebooks have been altered or changed in any way with respect to their condition since their acquisition?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, you don't know, or no they haven't been?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they haven't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to lead you to a completely different area, if I could. Was one of your objectives in evaluating these intercepts an effort to determine whether or not the material was genuine?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In doing that, was one of your efforts also to determine whether or not it was reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court generally, in terms of your efforts to determine whether or not the material was reliable, could you tell the Court generally what you did?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long process, and the information, as we've just discussed, came in at different points. So we started off working with the printed -- the printouts, that big binder of 550 pages or so, and began to log it, associate dates with conversations, where we were able to, and record participants, people who were speaking, if those were indicated, and we also recorded other significant -- other names that came up in the conversation -- that came up in the conversations, and also locations that came up in the conversations. We also summarised the conversations. So that we began to develop a knowledge of this body of material. Then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then as additional -- then as we started to work with the notebooks, we started to cross-reference the information in the notebooks with what we had from those original printouts, from those reports. And from there we were able to fill in more information about the dates. And we were able to see sometimes that there were lines missing at the bottom of those reports. It was really a constant process of cross-referencing and -- and making them -- and understanding and working with the material more and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to examine, I would say, third-party information or information that didn't original from the intercepts themselves?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us what kind of information that was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That came from other aspects of the ongoing investigation. It came from material from overhead imagery, for example, from media reports, from phone books, from captured military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Material -- material like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you or the people that were involved in this project undertake to corroborate the contents of these intercepted materials?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you do that in your effort to determine whether or not the material was reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- tell the Judges what kinds of factors did you look at in determining or assessing the reliability of this material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We looked at a lot of different things. We looked at internal consistency among -- between the reports and the notebooks. And then we started finding conversations that seemed to be recorded twice, and we -- initially we didn't understand how that could be the case. And we didn't understand that until we were able to learn that there were two sites from which this communication was being recorded. We looked at -- yeah, date reliability, how closely the -- the notebooks -- or the printouts mirrored what was recorded in the notebooks. It was all a process of -- of a lot of comparison and cross-referencing. And then, as -- as -- as we mentioned also looking at -- at third party, at outside sources to corroborate the information that was contained within -- independently corroborate the information that was contained within the intercepted material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you compare the information that you found in these intercepted materials with your general knowledge about circumstances of the case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you attempt to cross-reference or analyse -- you've mentioned that occasionally you came across conversations that seemed to have originated from two different sites?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you were able to cross-reference those conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you find certain identifiable consistencies between them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what kinds of consistencies you found and -- and whether or not you considered those consistencies in determining the reliability of the information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where -- sometimes the dates were the same, but sometimes also we didn't have dates on two or three of the conversations. But, for example, the times, the times would be very, very close. Sometimes identical, sometimes within a minute or two. The conversants, the participants speaking would be the same or -- and we would also find phrases, pieces of parts, sections of the conversations that were very, very close or -- or identical. So we knew that we were dealing -- that we -- or we -- we believed that we had the same conversation, but again at that particular time, we didn't understand how it was that we had the same conversation that was recorded either two times or sometimes three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In determining the -- in evaluating the reliability of this material originating from the two different sites, in terms of evaluating -- in terms of evaluating their reliability for your purposes, did you consider certain factors about them, such as how closely related they were physically or operationally or whether they shared certain information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we were able to begin speaking with the operators, we understood that there were two sites. And then that gave a whole lot more reliability to the -- to the process, because they were located at such distances and yet they were simultaneously recording the same thing. So, yes, that contributed also to the -- to the reliability of the -- of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you also undertake to interview or speak to the individual operators that had been identified in order to determine whether or not the material was genuine?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in doing so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think we need to clear -- clarify here whether she means to say that she spoke to all of them or to some of them. At least we need to know, more or less, how many of these intercept operators she spoke or they spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many of these intercept operators you spoke to or were spoken to by members that were involved in this process of verifying this information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke to them at -- at different points. In total I guess -- I mean it's hard for me to say off the top of my head, but during the time that I was with the Office of the Prosecutor, I guess that I would have -- or members of the -- members of the Prosecution team would have spoken to, I don't know, 15 or so operators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one further question. Were these 15 or so operators identified, chosen at random, and what was the source of your information as to the identities of these intercept operators that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We first -- we took the notebooks and we tried -- we focused on conversations that we considered to be important to the investigation. Taking those handwritten notes then we went to Tuzla and we tried to identify who those operators were, based on their handwriting. Taking the original notebooks with us, and showing them to the operators who were there and then also taking handwriting samples from them to be able to compare them to -- to the original notebooks. So it was an ongoing -- it was an ongoing process, but one that was fairly narrowly focused initially to the conversations that the Office of the Prosecutor thought were of most interest to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just another -- a further question. Were you given a list containing the names of the various intercept operators that worked the two locations, the northern and the southern one, at any time by the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During the course of these missions that you undertook to identify certain operators, did you -- you did this based upon the initial trip or did you do that based upon having gathered handwriting samples and performed some analysis on your own?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had performed -- we had worked with the material a lot before we contacted -- before we attempted to contact the intercept operators. So we knew the material quite well, and -- and then planned -- it was -- it was just a -- it was the next step, really, in working on the reliability of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that, in determining the reliability of this information, did you speak to the intercept operators or their commanders about the process itself?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the process itself, are there particular aspects of it that you considered in evaluating the reliability of the information contained in the intercepted material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what -- what you considered?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned that -- that they had -- that they had a process in place, that the operators were -- were told that they were to record exactly what they heard and that if they -- if they weren't sure about what they heard, that they should leave you know either a series of dots or indicate that a particular part of the conversation was incomprehensible or inaudible, that if they didn't know who the participants were, that they should indicate that by X and Y, 1 or 2, something like that, not to guess. Over the course of time, the operators indicated that they learned, by voice, that they were able to identify a number of the participants. But if the -- if names didn't appear in the body of conversations, then they were instructed to put those names in parentheses. And so those sorts of procedures, I guess, also -- also gave us more confidence in -- in the process. So you would often see an X and a Y with perhaps a name in parentheses, and to us that indicated that that's who they believed was speaking at the time, but again the name -- the name hadn't been mentioned in the conversation and so that was why it wasn't indicated as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to clarify one further point while we are at this. As I understand it, Ms. Frease is taking the two locations together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were different intercept operators from different units, say army, intelligence, police, national security or whatever. You have been giving us an indication as to what you were told to be the practice during these intercept operations. Was the practice the same across the board in the case of all the different kinds of operators, or were there sections that had something different in their -- in their practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the -- one of the units, for example, was much more consistent in writing down the dates, and in even indicating which operator, who it was that was recording that conversation. They would sign their names almost always at the bottom of those conversations. So there were those kinds of differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you remember which section or which unit adopted this practice or at least told you that they adopted this practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I say it in open court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did you receive information that all the units across the board, for example, employed the use of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in December of 1994 that they began to use notebooks in order to record conversations. And the commander at 2 Corps headquarters would number and date the notebooks and then they would be delivered, empty notebooks would be delivered, generally at the beginning of shifts and old ones would be picked up at the end of old shifts and taken back to their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to, for example, state security, do you know what their practice was with respect to the use of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have the practice of using notebooks. They -- they wrote conversations on, you know, bits of paper that they could find, and then typed them up and -- and send them forward. Sometimes they would type them up directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what would happen to these sheets of paper? Would they -- would they preserve them or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was told was that they burned them, they destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, with respect to the 21st Division, whether or not -- what their practice was with respect to the use of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would -- they used notebooks. They recorded the conversations in them and then they typed them up and sent them forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In consideration of the factors that you looked at in terms of evaluating the reliability of the material, did you look, for example, or consider whether or not this information was directly transcribed or transcribed off of a tape, for example? Did you consider that in determining or evaluating the reliability of this information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, do you know whether or not this information -- I guess I should take it by unit, but do you know whether or not this information that was recorded in the notebooks was directly transcribed, that is without it being recorded, right out of the -- straight off the head sets or it was recorded off of -- off of a recording that was transcribed based upon a recording that was -- if that was the practice? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the practice that the conversations were recorded on to tape and then -- and -- that the -- the time that the conversation started would be noted on a little piece of -- on a piece of paper and then later, sometimes immediately, it depended what the content of the conversation was and how important the operator thought the conversation was, but then either immediately or shortly thereafter the conversation would be transcribed from listening to the tape. That was the general practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the -- or did you learn, I should say, from your conversations with the operators, whether or not they were permitted to make assumptions or engage in analysis of the information that they were intercepting?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not -- they were not permitted to make assumptions. Nor did they engage in analysis. Their job was to record the information as accurately as they could -- as they could get it down. And -- and then to forward it to their headquarters, where it would then be analysed and subsequent action would be taken. But their job was -- was purely to record the information that was coming across.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, is that information that you've just relayed, was that based upon your conversations with individual operators in general or ...

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And were you able to verify or confirm that information with any -- any of their commanders or somebody in a position of authority?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that done in relation to the material that was transcribed by 2nd Corps operators?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what about in relation to the material that was transcribed by state security or as you called it, the police intercept operators located at the northern facility?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also for them. It was important to them to have the information and to forward it on to their headquarters. Sometimes it was very operationally important, and so to have the information recorded as accurately as possible was critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that the material was taped and then transcribed. Did you -- were you able to ascertain just in general terms, because it's impossible to say specifically, but just in general terms, how long a period of time for example would elapse between the time that an intercept was recorded and the time that it was transcribed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oftentimes during -- oftentimes it was really a matter of minutes. And sometimes we see differences, in fact, in the -- in the time that the intercept operator recorded in the notebook and then the time that the typist recorded on the typed version of that conversation. I'm sure you've come across examples of that where -- right, where an operator may say that a -- or wrote down that a conversation took place at for example 10.30, but the -- but the typist reported or recorded that it -- recorded 10.35, or 10.34, you know. So it was -- it was quickly. It was the same day, always, and usually within a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of these time discrepancies, as you've described them -- in your effort to evaluate the reliability of this information, were the time discrepancies you have indicated, 10.30 to 10.35, a dispositive factor in terms of the reliability of the information or was it one of several factors that you considered in terms of evaluating whether or not the particular communication was reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- yeah, I mean -- I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. Were you given an explanation for such discrepancies, as Mr. Vanderpuye has referred to them, which was acceptable enough to you to reach certain conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what were these explanations, if you could remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, simply that -- that -- and it was -- it was one -- it was one typist in particular who -- who changed the times a little bit from the time of the actual recording to the time that he actually typed it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever become privy to the reason why this particular --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- typist would do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. I think it's time to have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that it's a good time for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I could ask you how much more time do you require so that we plan ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I really have only one other area to take the witness through. I think it will take about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think when we left off we were talking about particular factors you considered and in that circumstance was relative to time that an intercept appeared to be transcribed in the notebook versus the time that it appeared to be typed or the time that was indicated in the typed transcription. When you came across these types of discrepancies would you consider whether or not there were additional errors or discrepancies between the notebook and the printouts in evaluating whether or not the information contained in it was reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is inquiring whether the second microphone should be on. It's on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so in determining or evaluating the reliability of the communication as a whole, which you would consider -- would you consider, I should say, more than whether or not there was a discrepancy in terms of the time or ...

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you know that your testimony today is limited and you will be coming back, I think, relatively shortly, to talk about some of the work that you are doing regarding the intercepts used in this particular case, but I would like to move ahead today, see how far we can get. I would like to direct your attention to another area, if I could. Now, in relation to your prior engagement with the Office of the Prosecutor, were you at some point asked to put together certain corroborative material regarding the intercepted material that had been received?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was that done in relation to the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that information also used in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just briefly explain to the Court, and to counsel, what that process entailed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the process of analysing the intercepted communication, we would -- when we came across information that we thought could be corroborated independently, we would highlight those conversations and set them aside. So when it came time, we -- we went through that material and -- in addition to other material, and then looked for independent material that could corroborate the -- the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And when you are talking about independent material, are you referring to military documents, as you have indicated before and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And are those documents that were provided to you by other members of the team involved in this process in some instances?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in other instances, were those documents that you came across on your own?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell the Court -- well, you know what, why don't we just go right into this. Did you prepare a -- and you have indicated that you did prepare some material regarding this, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have 65 ter 1074, please, brought up in e-court, if I may. While that's loading, could you just tell the Court what the nature of this material is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a compilation of a dozen intercepts and other material that independently corroborate those -- those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, does that represent the totality of the work you have done with respect to verifying the reliability of this intercept material or is it a -- really a sample, a representative sample of the type of work that was done in reviewing these -- that material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a representative sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us - I hope you have it on your screen - can you tell us what we have on the screen at this time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an index of the conversations, the intercepted conversations and what they discuss and then in addition what the corroborative material focuses on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And could you just describe generally the layout of this material? That is, here you have an index, and you've mentioned that there is a particular intercept in this corroborative material. Could you tell -- just so the Court has some familiarity with the way it's laid out, how it is that you've prepared this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. There are tab numbers, 1 through 12, I believe. The date of the intercepted conversation, and the time that was intercepted. In some cases there are more -- there are more than one conversation. And then the general subject of that conversation. So, for example, tab 1 is a telephone conversation between General Gobillard and General Gvero on the 11th of July at 1800 hours. The corroborative material would go directly to that conversation, but would have been from a third party. In this case, UNPROFOR notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That seems like a good place to start. I would like to focus your attention, and maybe we could go through three of these, so the Court has an idea or understanding of how it is organised and what process you engaged in. All right. Is it possible to go to page 2 on this document? Okay. Can you tell us what's on the screen now, what -- what that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a summary that I prepared of the conversation. It says "General Gobillard, acting commander of UNPROFOR, command for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo" and "General Gvero, assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs, VRS main staff," had a conversation which they discussed issues related to the takeover of the Srebrenica enclave, and I highlighted 13 points. It was a conversation that was intercepted by the State Security Service in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1995, at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn to the next page, please. Okay. Can you tell us -- well, I think we can see what this is. This appears to be a document that was prepared on the 11th of July. Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- they are notes taken by a staffer to General Gobillard. His signature is on the second page at the bottom. It's a tale of their notes from a telephone conversation between General Gobillard and General Gvero on the 11th of July, 1995. He recorded the time at 1810.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If I could, could you tell us what these -- well, there is a number one that's indicated on the -- on this piece -- on this document. And there are other numbers. Could we scroll down, please. Okay. One through seven on this page. Could you tell us what those mean?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be possible to also have the intercepted -- the intercept on the same screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can. All right. We can do it on the ELMO. All right. All right. Could I -- yes, we do. All right. Ms. Frease, do you have ERN ending 077 in front of you on the e-court system?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have ERN ending 080 -- or maybe I'm mistaken. Do you have the intercept that you referred to previously in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what the -- in the process of explaining what these numbers meant.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. They -- what they show are particular parts of the intercepted communication that the police recorded, and those parts of the conversation that correspond to the notes that were taken by General Gobillard's aide. And so the numbers essentially, you know, just match up between those two conversations. The notes on the one hand, and the -- the intercepted communication on the other. Number 1 indicates simply the date and time and the conversants. So before when I mentioned that the police always started their intercepted communication with a set phrase that says, "On the aforementioned day, while monitoring radio relay in the Pale direction on frequency 836000 megahertz at 1800 hours, we recorded a conversation between General Gvero and General Gobillard." And that information is reflected in point 1 of the notes that Major Fortin took. Point 2 reflecting -- it becomes self-evident, but General -- point 2 on the radio communication says it is now clear to me that General Gobillard gave the order for the shelling of the Serb positions. And point 2, I can't see it on the screen now, but point 2, if you can scroll down, I don't know, on the notes, or to the left, so that I can see the numbers. Sorry, the first document -- other direction. Yeah. There you go. Point 2, then there says General Gvero's first reaction that it was now clear -- and now the text is cut off for me, but essentially it follows the radio recording. Point 3, the same, and throughout those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so the numbers that you've indicated on both of these documents correlate with points that you considered in terms of verifying the accuracy and the reliability of the intercepted material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in it particular case you have indicated that the information was recorded by -- well, if you could just tell us who it was recorded by?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The State Security Services.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to General Gobillard, can you tell us who recorded the information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Fortin, I believe it was, his aide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: His signature block is indicated on the second page of that telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we could just go to the second page, so everybody could see what that is, and then we'll move on to the next.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to go through, you know, points 3 and 4 if that's of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I think it might be helpful to go through a few of them. Maybe some of the more salient points, that may be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You know what, let's take a look at tab number 6. That's page 45 in e-court. Maybe we can go through some of the points in this conversation. Okay. Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think certain of the accused do not receive the translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The translation of this document, you mean? Or interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let me check.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for pointing this out and also for having it clarified. Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure because I'm told that there is no translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you fine with the situation now? No, I see that Mr. Borovcanin -- yes. Can you explain your problem exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we don't have any of the documents in the language that we understand, not only this one, but from the very beginning.
