utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What we can do is, I suppose, use the same -- if it is possible to have the -- the two juxtaposed on the monitor, okay, that's fine. If it's not, we'll have one in English, either in e-court or on -- on the -- on the ELMO, and the other B/C/S text either on e-court or on the ELMO, so that they can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand it, there is not a B/C/S text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- of this particular binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, there is no translation of this. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The record should be clear that the intercepted material itself is obviously in B/C/S. The corroborative material is also to a great extent in B/C/S. Of course the -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not happy with the arrangement. As we tried to explain on previous occasions, there are certain rules that govern our procedure, meant to protect the rights of the accused that we would always respect. So the document that we have on e-court at the moment, it's 65 -- sorry, ERN 0119, is a very short one, three lines, basically, and that can be read out and automatically translated or interpreted in B/C/S, but it's our decision not to proceed with further questions referring to other such documents that have not been translated in B/C/S and made available to the parties, which can be followed by the accused for the time being, until you have a proper binder with the proper translations in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just in case there is a more practical solution, there are several of these documents, I understand. Perhaps the 65 ter number of these documents can be identified and one have a look at them and see whether it is practical to proceed with an interpretation or translation of them now, as we go along. I am not in a position to -- to know if it's practical or not. If it's practical, maybe we can save the day along those lines. If it's not, I mean the only way to deal with it is the way we indicated earlier on. You know -- you're familiar with these documents; we are not because we haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Certainly with respect to the ultimate tender or admissibility of the document itself, I think obviously given the objection that's raised, and I think it's a legitimate one, we will provide the translations. I think though, with respect to the two tabs that I wanted to proceed with, outside of the summaries that were prepared by the witness, they are translations of the documents that were relied upon in terms of assessing the reliability of the material. One of them is a photograph, and certainly the other is a translation of documents that were originally in B/C/S, and I think we can upload -- I think they are already uploaded on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What can be -- what can be made use of today in a manner which guarantees the ability of -- of the accused to follow the proceedings, it's okay. But we will have a hedge. You will encounter a hedge in the case of any other documents. What you can deal with in accordance or in conformity with our ruling, yes, by all means. What you cannot has to be postponed until a later date. In any case, Ms. Frease is returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can give it a try with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I had referred you initially to page 45 of the document that's on e-court. Could we turn to page 46 and 47. I think those are the two documents, one in English and one in B/C/S. All right. Do you recognise these particular documents, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you tell us what they relate to within the context of the binder that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are two conversations that relate to prisoners being detained at Nova Kasaba, at the stadium at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us if you were able to -- were you able to find any corroborative information relating to this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the two -- the two conversations, this is one of the two from the 13th of July at 1602.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another one, I believe, that is also included in the packet, that also makes reference to prisoners and being held at Nova Kasaba. In this first conversation at 1602, it says that they've got an extension down in Nova Kasaba. It's a conversation between X and Y, so the operator who recorded this didn't know who was speaking. X, three lines down, asks where Malinic's unit is, and says then that they said that there are over 1500 gathered at the stadium. And then reiterates two lines down that, yes, there are 1500 at the stadium in Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we look at pages 48 and 50, please.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another conversation that was recorded at 1730, also on the 13th of July, in which they talk about 6.000 being at three different points, roughly 1.500 to 2.000 at each location. And that -- if you could scroll down a little bit, and maybe go to the next page on the B/C/S version. They talk -- they mention Kasaba also in this conversation. And again it's a conversation between X and Y, so the -- the operator that recorded this didn't know who the conversants were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, obviously it was recorded at a different time than the other?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So can you tell the Court how it is this particular intercept is corroborative of the previous?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we used these to -- with over -- with overhead imagery, actually that we had, that we got from -- showing the soccer field at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July in which groups of prisoners were gathered. So these were two of the conversations that we used in order to -- well, we used the overhead imagery to corroborate these two conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we turn to page 54, please. Okay. Can you tell us what -- can you tell us what this is, this photograph?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an -- it's an -- an aerial image of Nova Kasaba, of the soccer field at Nova Kasaba. It's not a very clear picture, but what it indicates is that it was shot at about sometime around 1400 hours on the 13th of July in the -- in the soccer field. You can see a couple of groups of what were identified as -- by analysts as being groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the analyst determination that they were groups of people is what informs your assessment of the reliability of the information contained in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you able to determine if there were -- if there was additional corroborative material of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since I put this together, there has been additional information that's come in that helps to further corroborate the two previous intercepts and additional intercepts that all relate to the events around Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July at about 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have -- let's see, PO2361A and PO2361B shown in e-court, please. Do you recognise what's being displayed in e-court --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- now? Okay. Now, did you examine this particular -- first of all, for the record, could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a conversation that was intercepted by the army at 1400 hours on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And does that correspond to the aerial image that you previously testified about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of time -- what about in terms of location?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conversation mentions in the second line that they have over 1.000. I have it -- it says, "I have over 1.000." And then six lines down Y is speaking. This is a conversation between X and Y again. People who were talking were unknown. It says, "Well, they are down here at the soccer field."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is there some indication that the soccer field that is referred to in this particular intercept is the -- what is depicted in the aerial imagery?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we -- could I have P02362A and P02362B please shown in e-court. Okay. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure the translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1405, it should be. It should start -- and where is that? I think you might -- I think you have the second page of the first intercept that we looked at -- of the previous intercept that we looked at at 1400 hours, that's the second page of that intercept. So now we need the translation of this one at 1405. I have an ERN number, if it helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it will.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 7316. All right. We're going to try and locate that. I think, we have a linkage problem. ERN on the left part of the screen is 00927815. We're looking for 7816. Please excuse me. All right. We have a hard copy of it, if we can put it on the ELMO, maybe that will speed things along. And the document that's in B/C/S should be on this -- this appears to be the second page of that intercept, so I wonder if we could page back to 00778895. All right. I think maybe we've solved the problem. Can you tell us about this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one that was recorded also by the army at 1405 on the 13th of July, and it -- the participants are X and Y. X asked, "Where is that?" Y says, "Well, here at the soccer field." And then three lines down it says -- the English translation is, "Bro, don't take anymore. I'm going to send you an urgent telegram. Don't take anymore. Move it a bit. I will send you a telegram and explain everything." And then Y says, "Okay." X says, "Secure it well and the rest you will receive in a telegram. Don't do anything before that." Meaning before receiving the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain whether or not such a telegram exists and whether or not it's corroborative of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Was that telegram provided to you by members of the team working with you in verifying the reliability of this information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 00192 please displayed in e-court. Okay. Do you recognise -- do you recognise these documents or this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is for the record?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document that was sent by the forward command post of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment from a place called Borike at 1400 hours. That's the -- that's the time listed at the top of the document. It was sent -- however, there is a handwritten note at the bottom of it indicating the 13th of July, 1995 at 1510. It's a document that was written by the commander of that protection regiment, Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic and it is directed to the commander of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska army for his information. It's also directed to the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS for his information. And to the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and it is an order to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what points of comparison you have made that corroborate the intercepted material that you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first opening paragraph says that there are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba). This is Nova Kasaba and also in the intercepts is referred to as the football pitch or the football field. Prisoners are under the control of the army police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. So the fact that they talk about the -- the custody of 1.000 members in Kasaba was significant. The date is significant, and the time is significant. Also, just some of the text, some of the words that are used in the -- in the order comparing to the words used in -- in the intercept from 1405 on that same day are -- are very similar. And this order talks about prohibiting point 1 in the document, prohibiting access to all unauthorised individuals. And then -- well, shall I go through all four points? There are loose references that tie them together. First of all, that the time and the fact that the people in the conversation at 1405 are talking about the fact that they're going to send a telegram and not to act before receiving that telegram, and then having them move people away. And it is significant that in point 3 of the order it says that the commander of the military police battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in the area protected from sighting from the ground or the air. It then goes on in the last paragraph to say that once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order, he should contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders to verify if the proposal has been approved. I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could, I would like to take you to what you have in your index as tab 8. And that's page 60 of 65 ter 10 -- I mean 1074. Now, that is a summary that hasn't been translated, so I would ask if we could just go to page 61, which is the intercept itself in question. And 63 I think is where the B/C/S version of the intercept is. Okay. Do you recognise this -- wait a minute. I don't have the B/C/S version. Okay. All right. Do you recognise this particular intercept, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us about this one in relation to the work that you've done in preparing this binder?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a conversation that was intercepted on the 16th of July at 1358, and it relates to the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic needs 1500 [sic] litres of D2 diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you able to come up with information that corroborates this -- this request, this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if I could just maybe mention a couple of other points in this conversation. It's -- it's topped up a little bit that -- the line gets disconnected a couple of times, but it mentions lieutenant -- that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is at Palma, the -- and then -- that -- which is the -- the code-name for the Zvornik brigade and that he needs this -- this 500 litres of D2 urgently. I believe it's on the second page that they say -- if we could go to the second page of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And of the translation. The second page of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Should be page 62.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Right. If you -- if you look down towards the bottom of it, say about half a dozen lines, in parentheses, it says immediately after the end of the conversation, and then the next line down says, "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village, that's it. 500 litres." And it talks about -- up in the conversation earlier, it talks about that it's important for it to get there, otherwise, his work will stop. That's just a little bit above that line. At the time we knew that from testimony of another witness that there were executions happening in Pilica village on that day. The corroborative -- the independently sort of corroborative material that we used, maybe we can go to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on page 66 and 67.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was seized at the Zvornik Brigade by members of the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998, and it's a fuel log dated the 16th of July, 1995. That you'll see -- I think it's box 6 in the top left corner where it says "date." And then -- could you scroll back up to the top of the document. Yeah. Thank you. And then it -- it mentions needing 500 -- 500 litres of D2, and that it is going to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. That's in box number 15, that his name is indicated. And box number 14 gives the name -- right, the Drina Corps command as the recipient. Can you zoom up a little bit on the English translation. Yeah, thank you. So it was -- it was -- the name and addressee of the sender was Zvornik and it was as I said, going to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, 500 litres of D2. 300 -- it seems that 360 arrived and that 140 were sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, is there an indication on this particular document as to the location that the fuel was sent, other than the recipient of the fuel itself?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the other aspects of the document, that is the date, the recipient and the amount of fuel, are those the factors you considered in corroborating or verifying the reliability of the particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I will leave it at that for today. I don't think there is a need to go through the entire binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, Mr. Vanderpuye, and you, Ms. Frease. Of course we will need you again to return. And you will be advised accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, just -- Mr. President, the same rule applies. We will endeavour not to talk to her about her prior testimony, but for the upcoming testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. The situation remains as we established it last time Ms. Frease came to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go through some of the housekeeping matters that have surfaced since yesterday. Yes. Are you tendering any documents today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I thought I would wait until the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that was the procedure that we had adopted last time. I just wanted to make sure. Let's start with this one. Yesterday the Defence team for Colonel Beara filed a motion called, "Defence request for assistance re: Examination of a limited number of witnesses" with annexes A and B. Basically, what is being asked from Messrs. Ostojic and Meek is that we grant the Defence of Colonel Beara the assistance of Mr. Nebojsa Mrkic such that he has a limited right of audience to examine five to seven witnesses during the OTP case and seven to 10 witnesses during the Defence case so that the Defence can move more efficiently, et cetera. This has been intimated orally by Mr. Ostojic prior to the Christmas and New Years recess. And to my recollection, you had stood up, Mr. McCloskey, and intimated that you wouldn't oppose or that we would rather agree with such a request. So does any one of you wish to add anything to this, particularly in relation to the point whether it should be us that we should decide this or -- or the Registrar? I know that the Registrar has passed on the baby to us, but I would like to hear -- we'd like to hear some submissions in regard -- I don't know. Mr. Ostojic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think our motion and request orally made in December of last year was just to advise the Court that we did try to correctly contact the Registry with all the documentation, and me and my learned friend Mr. McCloskey have sat down and agreed, with respect to which witnesses they will be, because they keep shifting, we will sit in advance and make sure and ensure that Mr. McCloskey doesn't have an objection to the witnesses that Mr. Mrkic would potentially cross-examine and also those witnesses that we would call in our direct Defence case. I would just like to also add, we submitted his CV, his credentials. I think he has been in court, if not 100 per cent of the time, at least 90 per cent of the time. He is aware of the facts in the case. He has an excellent reputation back home as well as here. He is supported also by the ADC and Mr. Karnavas, specifically in my conversations with Mr. Karnavas. Also he has been able to translate and interpret for Mr. Meek with our client Mr. Beara. I think it's a good working relationship. It has functioned well given the Court's accelerated schedule. We think it would be necessary so that we don't have any delays, but also, in light of the fact that the Registry did defer to the Court, we think it was best to just bring it to the Court's attention and ask that leave from Your Honours here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, what is of concern to the Trial Chamber before we pass on to decide the issue is this: That although the bottom line and the Registrar's communication to you, Mr. Ostojic, is that the final decision according to the Registrar, whether to grant audience to a person other than counsel and allow him or her to cross-examine lies with the Chamber seized of the case, although he says that, in the previous paragraph, by reference to some instances to which you had referred in your communication with the Registrar, the Registrar says, "As to the two cases in which legal assistance were authorised to perform a cross-examination, I would like to emphasise that the Registrar, for the reasons outlined above," and I don't need to go into those, "had voiced his concerns and did not agree with the approach taken by the Chamber in question." So we would like you to sort of address the Trial Chamber as the following: The same breath, the Registrar is saying, when on previous occasion the Trial Chamber accorded or granted a legal assistant to cross-examine witnesses, that was not something that we digested well, meaning the Registrar, we didn't agree with it. We still don't agree with it. It's true that in his letter he is full of praise for the qualities of Mr. Mrkic, which we have no reason to doubt, and Mr. McCloskey also has no reason to doubt. But then, how are we going to overcome this -- this hurdle?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I suggest we could fire Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to address this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since, Mr. President, you raised it. Obviously, in one case, Mr. President, you were involved in that case, and the other one was a current case that is on trial in another courtroom. I believe, with all due respect to the Registry, that they should not get that intimately involved with running the courtroom and that it's Your Honour's decision as to what latitude or discretion we as the lawyers can have in order to efficiently present and to defend the case here. And I say respectly to the Registry, we've tried and we've been very courteous to them and they don't see it as we see it, but I don't know that they're intimately involved with the specific day-to-day process. So I think it's your decision, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And we are proceeding with our decision herewith. It will be an oral decision which will not be followed by a written one. So we are seized of a Defence request for assistance in the examination of a limited number of witnesses with annexes A and B, to with -- particularly by enabling or by authorizing legal assistance in Nebojsa Mrkic in the Beara Defence team to have a limited right of audience to examine five to seven witnesses during the OTP case or seven to 10 witnesses during the Defence case. We have heard submissions from the parties, including that of the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, Mr. McCloskey, who agrees with the motion of the Beara Defence team. The Trial Chamber has gone through the documentation, and having considered their submissions and the qualities of Mr. Mrkic and the interests of justice in this particular case, grants the motion. So that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I suppose Mr. McCloskey is going to tell you now tit for tat. There is a Prosecution motion filed also yesterday which runs into something like 76 pages that includes a lot of photocopies of transcripts and translations and typed versions thereof. The essence of the Prosecution motion is to have -- to be granted leave to amend the 65 ter witness list of witnesses, and permit the appearance and testimony of an additional two intercept operator persons, individuals. And in addition, the Prosecution is requesting for these two witnesses protective measures that are indicated in the motion itself. When do you plan, if granted, if this motion is granted, when will you be in a position to bring forward these two witnesses, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are in the process of speaking to them and we -- we hope within -- it's possible we could get them in before our -- our break. As you know, they are the result of the continuing search, especially for the southern area, while we had a list of who people were, we didn't know who did individual intercepts and these acts and conduct of intercepts. I don't know if counsel may consider some kind of stipulation, since their intercepts are few and the issues have been very clearly set out and -- and I can agree to most things counsel may bring up in cross-examination, such as a difference or that -- there are various things we have seen them bring out. So we're trying, but we have been trying all along with other witnesses and there are issues about pregnant cows and other things that are pretty serious, actually. I don't have the most immediate intelligence on that, but I get it hourly on our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any responses on the part of the Defence teams? Any of the Defence teams? Just trying to find in the body of the motion itself the details of the protective measures that you are asking for. They escape me as -- as I look through it. They escape me as I look through it. Is anyone checking from your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Pseudonym and face are the protective measures. We have not asked for voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Voice distortion, all right. Do I -- do -- do we take your silence as no objection? Yeah, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these two witnesses, I don't have any objections, but I do have an objection relating to the third witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The third -- which third one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'm talking about the second submission requesting the protective measures for another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's -- that's clear enough. So can we proceed with the -- yes, yes. Can we proceed with deciding this issue? Okay. So again the Trial Chamber is seized of a confidential Prosecution motion for leave to amend the witness list by adding two intercept operators as 92 ter witnesses. Such motion being filed on the 24th of January, 2007. Reference is made to the motion itself and to annexes A, B and C, which identify also these witnesses. The Trial Chamber has heard the submissions of the parties, also in relation to the protective measures being sought by the Prosecution for these two witnesses, namely, use of pseudonym and facial -- facial distortion. There being sufficient reason for granting the motion and no objections having been heard, the motion is hereby granted. This oral decision will not be followed by a written one. Okay. Now, there is a further Prosecution motion also filed yesterday, confidentially, requesting protective measures for three witnesses. The witnesses are identified in the motion itself. What is being sought by the Prosecution is the use of a pseudonym and face distortion for all these three witnesses. Does any one of the Defence teams wish to make submissions? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to tell the Trial Chamber that we are going to make a written response to the Prosecutor's proposal regarding the protective measures for Witness PW-101. We are going to submit this by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. When is this -- when are these witnesses planned to be called? We are talking of Witness 143.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Two of them were the intercept folks I mentioned earlier that I hope to get some information on. Then one of the -- the third is -- if I could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was saying that having heard Mr. Zivanovic, we will postpone our decision until we have had an opportunity to go through his written filing, planned for tomorrow. Since there are inherent time constraints considering the proximity of the testimony of these witnesses, we are imposing on you, Mr. McCloskey, in case you wish to reply to Mr. Zivanovic's written filing, a deadline of Monday and not later. The same applies to any other Defence team that wishes, like Mr. Zivanovic, to raise their concerns or objections in relation to this motion. You will have until the end of business of tomorrow, Friday, to do that. And again, Prosecution will have until the end of business on Monday to respond, if it so wishes. All right? And that disposes of this motion as well. And we come now to this other motion that was filed yesterday by Mr. Zivanovic for Colonel Popovic. It's a request for extension of time regarding the 17 January 2007 order regarding intercept communications. Mr. Zivanovic is basically asking that the deadline of the 2nd February, in his opinion, simply does not allow the Defence to digest the evidence of the above-mentioned, or the MUP and particular division operators to whom he refers in his motion, as well as those witnesses to -- scheduled to testify after the said date of the 2nd of February. Mr. Zivanovic refers us to a previous statement that we made, namely, that we would -- we plan to rule on the admissibility of intercept evidence when all the evidence on them has been led by the Prosecution. And according to him, the order that we gave imposing the 2nd February deadline is incongruent with our previous statement. I will not ask you to explain why it would be incongruent with that previous statement, because that previous statement refers to the ruling and to nothing else. But what is the Prosecution's position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Normally, Mr. President, I -- I'm not very pushy about deadlines like this, so I -- I don't really have any serious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not like us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- objections. But -- but in terms of intercepts, two Trial Chambers have looked at much of the same material. This material has been available forever and ever. We have three more army intercept operators to testify, but as you know, that's very repetitive and the material they will testify with is clear. Ms. Frease is almost finished. The last chapter of her testimony will be just talking about the collection of intercepts that we have put together for this trial and what she has done to help collect them. So that's the material that -- that may be heard after your February 2nd date, just to put you in the factual context. As for -- I won't take a position either way. I'll leave that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, do you wish to maintain your motion or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stand by the proposal that I made, and I think it will not have any effect on the proceedings. I would just like to underscore that besides what I said, I also asked the Prosecution to state clearly whether all the material relating to the intercepts has been disclosed to the Defence in any form, including the placement of it on the EDS. I still haven't received a response. It's quite difficult to submit a motion like this, as you specified in your order, without having a clear picture of if what I manage to find so far is actually all that there is, relating to this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. As in the case of every other motion, of course we have had the opportunity to discuss amongst ourselves, and we do have some concerns about your motion, because I think it's based on a misconception or misunderstanding of our previous order. In fact, I invite Judge Prost to address you on -- on this, hoping that it will make things clearer. Yeah, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we wanted you to take into consideration the following in determining whether you need to maintain your request. Because perhaps -- perhaps you weren't clear on the -- the effect of our order, what we were seeking in the order. The Defence teams have all objected to the admissibility of all the intercepts, which obviously we consider a very important issue. So far, however, the Chamber has really no indication as to the basis, as to the underlying basis for the objections other than some general statements that are in the filings and have been made, and some comments from counsel during the course of the proceedings. Having now heard several weeks of evidence, we assume that the Defence must know at this stage at least some indication of the basis, the types of objections that are going to be made. And we are looking to have those articulated to us to assist us in dealing with what is a very critical issue. So that's what we're looking for at this stage is an outline of the basis of the objections. But we reiterate, we are not seeking full arguments on the evidence at this time, and the Defence will certainly have an opportunity to make those kinds of submissions before we make any kind of ruling on this issue. At this point though, we are just looking for some guidance from the Defence teams on the nature of the arguments, and in that context, we think the deadline that we set was quite a reasonable one for that kind of information. So we would ask you to take that into consideration and we can come back to this perhaps next week and just see if there is a need to extend the deadline in light of that. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can assure Mr. Zivanovic that you will find us reasonable at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will ask you about whether you maintain or reiterate your position this coming Monday again and then if -- if you do, we'll -- we'll proceed with our decision, which will be an oral one. Now, we are anxious to know what we are going to do tomorrow, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we lost that -- that witness that we thought would take up the whole day, I have been trying to find someone for tomorrow, but given -- even if I had willing people, there is this four-day visa requirement. The short answer is I don't have anyone for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any business that we could transact? For example, I don't know, I heard you state yesterday that you had some informal consultations with Mr. Ostojic in relation to the aerial images.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The -- the nature of -- of the case thus far is that there's so much -- we don't really even have anything to argue about at this point that we could use your help on. Mr. Ostojic and I seem pretty close to the aerial image situation, and -- and Mr. Bourgon is even -- I can't get him to argue with me. Although I'm sure he could think up something, but we're at a loss. I'm sorry. And I just meant that in good taste. I didn't mean to upset you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you don't even leave me space to act as an agent provocateur. I can't even do that. Let's do it this way: Maybe you can rethink this whole matter. We are at your disposal. It's not a day of -- for us, there are various issues, various motions outstanding that we will be dealing with. We will be here, like I'm sure every one of you. If there is any business that we can transact tomorrow in open court, then please do let us know. We are at your disposal. We will be here and the courtroom is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have been in discussions with -- with Ms. Nikolic about some witness issues which I think she may want to discuss. We have been hustling to try to get witnesses for next week, and we have managed to -- looks like we've done that. So far I was able to -- we had a gap on Wednesday but last night I was able to talk to Hilga Bromborg and he has been willing to drop everything he is doing next week and come from Norway to testify about his report about the missing. And I've had discussions with Ms. Nikolic about that and we have -- and she has asked me, and she can of course speak for herself, if there was a -- if there is some way we could work with that so they would have time to cross-examine the witness later. With Mr. Nikolic here, we believe we can put in some witnesses and put Mr. Bromberg off, but of course that depends on Mr. Nikolic's ability to be here. That's where we are on that -- on that point. And I would ... [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is sure that you are all doing your best to make the best use possible of the resources that are available. And the -- including time availability. So we stand adjourned -- not until tomorrow then until Monday. Monday we will be sitting in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
